claim_1.claim: A firm should trust its own people's judgement that AI is speeding them up, rather than wait to measure it.

claim_2.claim: An SME should run its AI on small models it controls rather than on frontier models it rents.
claim_2.shortfall_reason: CFA roundtable can fill NAS (controlled pipeline comparison) or NAW (podcast genre) but not both without breaking CL-2; whichever cell it takes, the other stops at 3. GDPval was dropped from NAS as an argument from silence (it never tested a small/open model). BFCL was removed from NAS because it is the same paper as AS#1. Rent-side weak advocacy is structurally scarce: Nadella, Jensen Huang and the BBC adviser all turn out A-leaning.
claim_2.caveat: NAW is three-quarters Amazon (two AWS events + Jassy) plus Google once. The rent-side case in this corpus is made almost entirely by hyperscalers, because every non-vendor candidate (Nadella, Jensen Huang, BBC adviser) argues A-leaning. Cell is usable but monotone; one non-vendor open-web voice would strengthen it. Separately, both strong cells rest on benchmark transfer — no source measures an SLM agent against an LLM agent on the same task under the same harness.

claim_3.claim: An SME's first AI project should make its existing staff faster rather than remove steps from a process.
claim_3.shortfall_reason: NAS is structurally unfillable: per automation-vs-augmentation, pure automation removes the worker so per-worker productivity stops being a coherent outcome, and randomised/population designs can only stock the augmentation side. A measurement asymmetry, not a corpus gap.
claim_3.note: NAS filled on the second pass. All four disagree by showing AUGMENTATION FAILING, not automation succeeding. The corpus still has no head-to-head study where automating a step beat assisting the worker on the same task, and automation-vs-augmentation explains why (automation dissolves the per-worker outcome). Sufficient for the instrument; worth briefing deliberately.

corrections_applied.what: Anthropic Economic Index latest augmentation/automation split

corrections_applied.from: paraphrase '3x more with the same resources, never a catalyst for layoffs'
corrections_applied.to: verbatim: 'if we could do 3x more with the same resources, we will do 3x more; that would never be the catalyst for layoffs' - catalyst is revenue, 'not AI'

headline_findings: Claim 2's NAW cell is three-quarters Amazon — the rent-side case is made almost entirely by hyperscalers because every non-vendor candidate argues the other way.
Claim 3's NAS cell fills, but all four disagree by showing augmentation failing rather than automation succeeding; no head-to-head automate-vs-assist study exists, and per the corpus probably cannot.
First-pass recommendations to drop claim 3 and to call claim 2 short are both WITHDRAWN.
Method: broad retrieval finds topics; cell-shaped queries find cells; a grep over frontmatter tags found what eight semantic queries missed.
The same source reads differently per claim — METR was a claim-1 source and became one of the strongest claim-3 NAS sources.
